title: The Gate of Tongues and the Burned Libraries: Comenius from Moravia to the Walloon Chapel
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Orphan of the Moravian Slopes

stops.name: Nivnice, the mill and the disputed birth
stops.date_confidence: Date attested (Comenius Museum, mjakub.cz; encyclopedia.com). Birthplace unresolved: the museum states plainly that the evidence does not permit a unique answer among Nivnice, Uhersky Brod, and Komna. Coordinates corrected to Nivnice village per cs.wikipedia (48.9746, 17.6476); the research pool's 48.9647, 17.6444 lies about 1.2 km south of the village.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of March a son is born to Martin Komensky and his wife Anna, and named Jan Amos. Three Moravian places claim the birth. Nivnice, whose name he later attaches to his own on title pages as Nivnicensis. Uhersky Brod, where the family lives. Komna, the village his grandfather governed as magistrate and from which the surname itself descends. Since 1993 the marked monument has been a mill at Nivnice, Bartkuv mlyn number 99, standing on the likeliest of the three. No birth record survives from any of them.
suggested_refs: Bartkuv mlyn no. 99 at Nivnice, cultural monument marked as his probable birthplace since 1993

stops.name: Uhersky Brod, both parents dead within the year
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (mjakub.cz); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The order of the two deaths inside the year is not recorded.
stops.campa: Martin and Anna Komensky both die inside a single year, and the boy is twelve. He leaves the town with no property and no father's trade, and is placed with an aunt, Zuzana Nohalova, at Straznice. Uhersky Brod holds its claim on him anyway, on the strength of family residence and a later epitaph tradition rather than any register. Three centuries on, the Comenius Museum will be built here, holding the archive from which most of what is known about him is read.
suggested_refs: Muzeum Jana Amose Komenskeho, Uhersky Brod, custodian of the biographical apparatus

stops.name: Straznice, the aunt's house and the first school
stops.date_confidence: 1605 attested for the Straznice school (mjakub.cz); month unknown, defaulted. The burning of the town by Bocskai's troops is given by the same source and is not separately dated there.
stops.campa: His aunt takes him in and he is enrolled in the school of the Unity of the Brethren, a church of scattered congregations that keeps the most disciplined schools in the Czech lands and its own press at Kralice. He learns to read the Brethren's Bible in the Brethren's Czech, the prose that will still be his instrument fifty years later in Amsterdam. The household does not last: troops raised in the Bocskai uprising burn Straznice, which is the second home he has had in two years.
suggested_refs: The Kralice Bible, six volumes, the Brethren's Czech scripture he learns to read here

stops.name: Prerov, Latin at sixteen
stops.date_confidence: 1608-1611 attested (mjakub.cz); month unknown, defaulted. The Great Didactic chapter heading quoted below is from Keatinge's 1896 translation and is placed here for its subject, not because Comenius wrote it at Prerov.
stops.campa: He enters the higher Brethren school at sixteen, late for a clerical career by the standards of the day, and takes his first Latin from Tomas Dubina. Bishop Jan Lanecky and Karel the Elder of Zerotin, the greatest Protestant magnate in Moravia, between them find the money for what follows. The boy who begins Latin at an age when others have finished it will argue for the next fifty years that the language is taught in the wrong order and at the wrong speed. He stays three years.
stops.quote: A man can most easily be formed in early youth, and cannot be formed properly except at this age.
stops.quote_source: The Great Didactic, chapter VII heading, tr. M. W. Keatinge (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The Brethren Latin school at Prerov, where he is both late pupil and, six years later, rector

segments.name: Herborn, Heidelberg, and the Walk Home

stops.name: Herborn, Alsted and the encyclopedic method
stops.date_confidence: Herborn years 1611-1613 attested (mjakub.cz; encyclopedia.com); month unknown, defaulted. The two disputations of 1612 are tagged [R] in the research pool, from the museum's index of works. The transmission of Ramon Llull's combinatorial art through Alsted is a dossier-led lead that could not be independently confirmed against ramon_llull.journey.json; treat that line as reconstruction, not attestation.
stops.campa: At the Reformed academy in Nassau he studies under Johann Piscator, Heinrich Gutberleth, and above all Johann Heinrich Alsted, who is assembling a single ordered encyclopedia of all knowledge and who reads Ramon Llull's combinatorial art as a working instrument rather than a curiosity. From Alsted the young Moravian takes two things he never afterward puts down: the conviction that everything known can be arranged into one system, and a chiliast's calendar in which that system arrives just before the end of the world. His first printed pieces, two academic disputations, come off a Herborn press in 1612.
suggested_refs: J. H. Alsted, Clavis artis Lullianae (Strasbourg, 1609), and his Encyclopaedia septem tomis distincta (Herborn, 1630)

stops.name: Heidelberg, Pareus and a bought Copernicus
stops.date_confidence: 1613-1614 attested (mjakub.cz; encyclopedia.com); month unknown, defaulted. The purchase of a Copernicus manuscript and the walk home through Nuremberg and Prague are tagged [R]: the Comenius Museum itself reports them as biographical tradition and cautions that the manuscript's identity and later fate cannot be established.
stops.campa: He moves to Heidelberg and studies under David Pareus, the Reformed theologian who spends his career arguing that the Protestant confessions can be brought back into one church, and completes a theological disputation there. Tradition holds that he spends his last money on a manuscript of Copernicus's De revolutionibus, and that he walks home to Moravia afterward by way of Nuremberg and Prague. Neither the manuscript nor the road appears in anything he wrote himself. Pareus's irenicism appears in almost everything he writes for the next fifty-six years.
suggested_refs: David Pareus, Irenicum sive de unione et synodo evangelicorum (Heidelberg, 1614)

stops.name: Prerov, rector at twenty-two
stops.date_confidence: Return to Moravia and headship of the Prerov school 1614-1617 attested (mjakub.cz); month unknown, defaulted to mid-year to place the stop after the Heidelberg studies. Theatrum universitatis rerum is attested as begun in this period and never completed.
stops.campa: He comes back at twenty-two to the school where he learned his own Latin and runs it until 1617. He begins collecting material for a Czech encyclopedia, Theatrum universitatis rerum, meant to hold everything there is, Alsted's project transplanted into a language spoken by perhaps three million people. He never finishes it, and the drafts of it burn at Fulnek in 1623, six years after he leaves this school. Meanwhile he teaches grammar to boys who started younger than he did.
suggested_refs: The surviving fragments of Theatrum universitatis rerum, begun at Prerov

segments.name: Fulnek, and the War That Takes It

stops.name: Zeravice, ordained at the synod
stops.date_confidence: The research pool gave year and place only; cs.wikipedia (Zeravice, okres Hodonin) supplies the exact synod date of 25 April 1616 and the figure of thirty-two men ordained, the twenty-four-year-old Comenius among them. Coordinates corrected to 49.0229, 17.2373; the pool's 49.2019, 17.2828 was about 20 km off.
stops.campa: On the twenty-fifth of April the Unity of the Brethren holds a synod in this Moravian village and ordains thirty-two men to its ministry. He is twenty-four. The church receiving him has been legal in the Czech lands for seven years, since Rudolf II's Letter of Majesty granted the non-Catholic estates their liberty of religion in 1609. Every man ordained in this room will be an outlaw within twelve years, and no legal Brethren synod will meet on Czech soil again for three hundred.
suggested_refs: Rudolf II's Letter of Majesty, 9 July 1609, the legal ground under this ordination

stops.name: Fulnek, pastor, rector, beekeeper
stops.date_confidence: 1618-1621 at Fulnek attested (mjakub.cz; en.wikipedia, 'Fulnek', which states he lived and worked here in those years); month unknown, defaulted. Coordinates corrected to Fulnek town, 49.7125, 17.9033; the research pool's 49.5875, 17.7047 lay about 22 km southwest, in a different place. The pool's identification of the museum with the Brethren house at namesti Komenskeho 12 is not confirmed: en.wikipedia places the Comenius Memorial in Knurr's Palace.
stops.campa: He is sent to Fulnek on the estate of Jan Skrbensky of Hriste as pastor of the Brethren congregation and rector of its school. He marries Magdalena Vizovska; two sons are born. In the same year the Bohemian Estates throw the emperor's regents from a window of the Prague castle, and the war that empties Central Europe begins two hundred kilometres away. This is the only settled household he will have in seventy-eight years, and it lasts about two. He preaches, teaches, maps the country, keeps bees.
stops.quote: All the young of both sexes should be sent to school.
stops.quote_source: The Great Didactic, chapter IX heading, tr. M. W. Keatinge (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The Brethren house at Fulnek, rebuilt as a prayer house in 1612, and the Comenius Memorial in Knurr's Palace

stops.name: Fulnek, the town sacked
stops.date_confidence: White Mountain, 8 November 1620, attested. The occupation and devastation of Fulnek is given by mjakub.cz and dated there across 1620-1621; en.wikipedia's Fulnek article carries nothing about an imperial or Spanish occupation or a burning, so that detail rests on the museum alone. Comenius was at Fulnek, not at the battle: the White Mountain field is named here as cause, not staged as a stop.
stops.campa: On the eighth of November the army of the Bohemian Estates is broken in about two hours on the White Mountain outside Prague, and the Czech Reformation loses its war in a single afternoon. Imperial troops reach Fulnek afterward and devastate the town, the Brethren school, and the church. He is a non-Catholic minister in a country where that has just become a crime. He goes into hiding, leaving his wife and two small sons behind. He does not see the house again.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Bila Hora west of Prague, 8 November 1620

stops.name: Velke Losiny, the death of Magdalena and the sons
stops.date_confidence: The deaths in 1622 are attested (mjakub.cz), which does not establish where the family was; the source itself does not locate them. The Zerotin shelter here is hedged to [R]: mjakub.cz says only that he hid in the Moravian mountains and then in the Velke Losiny area, and cs.wikipedia's Velke Losiny article names neither Comenius nor Karel the Elder of Zerotin for 1622. Coordinates corrected to 50.0319, 17.0406. The Vikstejn refuge named in the campa is local tradition only, and the castle stands in the Nizky Jesenik, not the Oderske vrchy as the research pool had it.
stops.campa: He is thirty. Eighteen months ago he was pastor at Fulnek with a wife and two small sons. He is hidden through these months on ground belonging to Karel the Elder of Zerotin, who paid for his schooling and now pays to keep him alive: first in the hills of the Nizky Jesenik near the castle of Vikstejn, then in the Losiny country. Magdalena and both boys die while he is in hiding, probably of plague. He is not with them, and the record does not say where they were.
suggested_refs: Vikstejn castle above the Moravice near Radkov, one of the refuges local tradition assigns him

stops.name: Fulnek, the books burned in the square
stops.date_confidence: Tagged [R] in the research pool: mjakub.cz reports the public burning of his library and manuscript drafts in the Fulnek square and cautions that precise responsibility is not fully documented, though the destruction itself is. He was in hiding elsewhere and learned of it; the stop is pinned to where the books were. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Word reaches him that his library and his manuscript drafts have been carried into the Fulnek square and burned in public. The Theatrum universitatis rerum goes into the fire, and the map of Moravia, and the notebooks of Prerov and Fulnek. It is the first of two libraries he loses to fire; the second is thirty-three years off. Who ordered this one is not documented with the certainty the destruction itself carries. The popular version names the Jesuits, and the record does not reach that far.
stops.quote: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity!
stops.quote_source: The Labyrinth of the World and the Paradise of the Heart, chapter XXXIII, tr. Count Lutzow (1901); Comenius gives the line to Solomon inside the allegory he is writing this same year
suggested_refs: The town square of Fulnek, site of the 1623 burning

segments.name: The Labyrinth and the Errand for the Unity

stops.name: Brandys nad Orlici, the Labyrinth written
stops.date_confidence: 1623 composition under protection at Brandys attested (mjakub.cz); month unknown, defaulted to mid-year. Coordinates corrected to 50.0020, 16.2853 per cs.wikipedia; the research pool's 49.9908, 16.3439 sat about 4.5 km east of the town, in open country. First printing 1631.
stops.campa: Sheltered under Zerotin's protection in this small town on the Orlice, he writes Labyrint sveta a raj srdce. A pilgrim is fitted with a bridle of meddling and spectacles of illusion and walked through the city of the world: the tradesmen, the scholars, the soldiers, the married, the ruling, the dying, all of it counterfeit and all of it loud. He finds nothing worth choosing anywhere in it and turns inward, into the paradise of the heart. He has just lost everything the book says is not worth having. The book waits eight years to be printed.
stops.quote: When I had attained that age at which the difference between good and bad begins to appear to the human understanding, I saw how different are the ranks, conditions, occupations of men, the works and endeavours at which they toil; and it seemed most necessary to me to consider what group of men I should join, and with what matters I should occupy my life.
stops.quote_source: The Labyrinth of the World and the Paradise of the Heart, chapter I, tr. Count Lutzow (1901), archive.org text
suggested_refs: The Comenius memorial and the Labyrinth trail at Brandys nad Orlici

stops.name: Brandys nad Orlici, entered in the town books
stops.date_confidence: 1624 marriage attested (mjakub.cz). Place corrected from the research pool's vague 'Bohemia/Moravia' to Brandys specifically: cs.wikipedia records that the marriage to Dorota Cyrillova is entered in the Brandys town books. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He marries Marie Dorota Cyrillova, daughter of a senior Brethren minister, and the Brandys town books write it down. She will be his wife for twenty-four years, through the frontier crossing, Leszno, London, Elbing, and the Peace of Westphalia. He is thirty-two, a widower, an outlawed priest of a proscribed church living on a nobleman's charity in a town where he cannot legally preach. A municipal clerk enters the marriage in the ordinary register the town keeps for its own residents.
suggested_refs: The Brandys nad Orlici town books, in which the 1624 marriage is recorded

stops.name: Szprotawa, the prophet Christoph Kotter
stops.date_confidence: The research pool dated the whole diplomatic route to 1625 in its chronology and the Hague audience to 1626 in its geography; mjakub.cz gives 'diplomatic journeys 1625-1626'. The internal inconsistency is not resolved here: the route is spread across 1625-1626 in date order. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: In Silesia he meets Christoph Kotter, a tanner who has been receiving visions in which the House of Austria falls and the exiled are brought home. Comenius takes the visions down, has them translated, and treats them as intelligence. He will do the same with Kristina Poniatowska and later with Mikulas Drabik, and he will be mocked for it for three hundred years. The Unity is scattered, its press is being carried across a border in pieces, and a tanner's dreams are the only source anywhere that says the Czechs come back.
suggested_refs: Lux in tenebris (1657), Comenius's collected edition of the Kotter, Poniatowska, and Drabik revelations

stops.name: Wroclaw, the Kralice press carried out
stops.date_confidence: Attested (mjakub.cz) as part of the 1625-1626 errand for the Unity, which the same source routes through Gorlitz, Sprottau, Leszno, Berlin, and The Hague. Month unknown within the period, defaulted to place the stop in sequence.
stops.campa: He is thirty-three and traveling for the church now: to Gorlitz, to Berlin, through the Silesian towns, arranging where the exiles will settle and asking Protestant courts for money and shelter. Two salvage operations run alongside the diplomacy. Karel the Elder of Zerotin's library is got out of Moravia. The press of Kralice, on which the Brethren printed their Czech Bible in six volumes, is carried out in pieces and set up again in Wroclaw, ahead of the confiscations.
suggested_refs: The Kralice press, moved to Wroclaw for safekeeping in 1625

stops.name: The Hague, prophecy delivered to the Winter King
stops.date_confidence: The audience with Frederick V is attested (mjakub.cz), dated 1626 in the research pool's geography lens and 1625 in its chronology lens; the museum's own framing is 'diplomatic journeys 1625-1626'. 1626 is used, the contradiction recorded. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He crosses into the Dutch Republic and is admitted to the exiled court of Frederick V of the Palatinate, who reigned in Bohemia for one winter and has been in Holland since White Mountain. Comenius has been a year on the road for the Unity by now, through Gorlitz, Sprottau, Leszno, and Berlin. Two men who have lost the same country stand in one room. He hands the deposed king the written predictions of a Silesian tanner: the Habsburgs fall, the exiles return. Nobody present treats this as a curiosity.
suggested_refs: Frances Yates, The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972), on the Palatine court and the political aftermath of its defeat

segments.name: The Last Bohemian Winters, and the Gate of Tongues

stops.name: Bila Tremesna, the knight's fortress
stops.date_confidence: 1626-1628 residence given by mjakub.cz; cs.wikipedia lists a Comenius memorial and monument in the village but names neither Jiri Sadovsky of Sloupno nor the residence, so that detail rests on the museum alone. Coordinates corrected to 50.4447, 15.7411; the research pool's 50.4197, 15.8236 lay about 7 km southeast. Month unknown, defaulted. The Renewed Land Ordinance dates given in the campa are corrected: the pool conflated the Ordinance with the emigration patent.
stops.campa: He lives mainly here for two years, in the fortified house of the Brethren knight Jiri Sadovsky of Sloupno, in the foothills of the Krkonose. From this base he moves among the last Protestant strongholds of northeastern Bohemia while the emigration is organized around him. The Renewed Land Ordinance is issued for Bohemia in May 1627 and for Moravia in May 1628; a separate imperial patent of 31 July 1627 gives the non-Catholic estates the choice of conversion or departure. He is already packing.
suggested_refs: Ferdinand II, Obnovene zrizeni zemske, Bohemia 10 May 1627 and Moravia 10 May 1628; the emigration patent of 31 July 1627

stops.name: Vlcice, the Zilvar library
stops.date_confidence: The Bodinus reading in Adam Zilvar's library comes from the research pool's chronology, drawing on mjakub.cz; cs.wikipedia confirms only that the Zilvar of Silberstein family held the village from the fifteenth to the seventeenth century, and adds a last-night-in-Bohemia tradition that it itself marks 'citation needed'. Neither claim is securely attested; both are recorded, neither adjudicated. Coordinates corrected to 50.5625, 15.8217; the pool's 50.5719, 15.7292 lay about 6.6 km west. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: In the library of Adam Zilvar of Silberstein he reads Elias Bodinus's Didactica oder Lehrkunst, a German treatise on the art of teaching. Something in it lodges. Within two years, in a Polish town, he begins writing his own didactic, and within eleven it is a Latin system claiming to teach all things to all men. The village also keeps a tradition that he spent his last night in Bohemia here. Zaclerz keeps the same tradition, ten kilometres north, and the two cannot both be right.
suggested_refs: Elias Bodinus, Didactica oder Lehrkunst, read in the Zilvar library

stops.name: Horni Branna, the girl who sees
stops.date_confidence: Attested (mjakub.cz) within the 1626-1628 residence; month and year within the period not fixed by the source, defaulted to order the segment. Lux in tenebris, named in the campa, is published in 1657 and postdates this stop.
stops.campa: At the castle of Vaclav Zaruba of Hustirany he encounters Kristina Poniatowska, a young woman of the Brethren circle who falls into trances and speaks. He takes down her revelations as she gives them, and will print them thirty years later alongside Kotter's and Drabik's in the collection Lux in tenebris. Learned Europe will hold this against him: the man who wants all knowledge ordered by method also keeps a clearing house for visionaries. He sees no contradiction.
suggested_refs: Zaruba castle at Horni Branna; the Poniatowska revelations as printed in Lux in tenebris

stops.name: Zaclerz, the last night in Bohemia
stops.date_confidence: Date attested (mjakub.cz). Location corrected: the research pool placed the crossing at 50.2, 16.55 near Nachod, about 70 km from the documented site. cs.wikipedia (Zaclerz) records the Ruzovy palousek memorial on the spot where Comenius crossed the Czech frontier into emigration on 4 February 1628, and that he spent his last night in Bohemia in Protestant Zaclerz on his road to Leszno. This conflicts with the Vlcice last-night tradition; both are recorded, neither adjudicated. Coordinates are approximate to the town.
stops.campa: On the fourth of February he crosses out of the Czech lands with his family and a column of Brethren emigrants, through the snow of the Krkonose passes toward Poland. A meadow above Zaclerz is marked as the place. He is thirty-five. He will live another forty-two years, in Poland, England, Sweden, Prussia, Hungary, and the Dutch Republic, and be buried in a Walloon chapel in a Dutch garrison town, and he never sets foot in Bohemia or Moravia again.
suggested_refs: The Ruzovy palousek memorial above Zaclerz, marking the frontier crossing of 4 February 1628

stops.name: Leszno, the school of the exiles
stops.date_confidence: Arrival in Leszno February 1628 and the teaching, rectorship, and composition of the Czech Didaktika there are attested (mjakub.cz; en.wikipedia, 'Leszno'). Month set to March to place the stop after the 4 February crossing. Didactica magna is composed in stages 1627-1638 and first printed in 1657.
stops.campa: The town is a Polish magnate's foundation with a Brethren community already generations old, and it absorbs the new Czech emigration. He teaches in the higher school, then becomes its rector. He writes the Czech Didaktika here, in the language of a country he has just been expelled from, for schools that no longer exist. He will translate and enlarge it into Latin as Didactica magna, and the Latin version, addressed to nobody in particular, will still be in print four hundred years later.
stops.quote: We venture to promise a Great Didactic, that is to say, the whole art of teaching all things to all men, and indeed of teaching them with certainty, so that the result cannot fail to follow.
stops.quote_source: The Great Didactic, 'Greeting to the Reader,' section 3, tr. M. W. Keatinge (1896), archive.org (Cornell copy)
suggested_refs: The Brethren gymnasium at Leszno; the Czech Didaktika, later Didactica magna

stops.name: Leszno, Janua linguarum reserata
stops.date_confidence: 1631 Leszno printing per the Comenius Museum bibliography; encyclopedia.com gives 1633 for a variant printing. The two are not reconciled here and the museum's 1631 is used for the original. Month unknown, defaulted. In the same year an outbreak in the town prompts a short tract of his against abandoning the sick and trading in infected animals, tagged [R] in the research pool.
stops.campa: The Gate of Tongues Unlocked comes off a Leszno press: a hundred short chapters of graded sentences about things, water and fire and trades and the parts of the body, through which the Latin arrives as a by-product of learning what the world contains. The old order of the schools is inverted. The boy is not made to memorize declensions first and permitted to meet the world afterward. Translations follow so fast across Europe that within a few years an exile with no country and no salary is being read in schoolrooms that have never heard of the Unity of the Brethren.
stops.quote: The exact order of instruction must be borrowed from nature.
stops.quote_source: The Great Didactic, chapter XIV heading, tr. M. W. Keatinge (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: Janua linguarum reserata (Leszno, 1631) and its early translations

stops.name: Leszno, bishop and scribe of a church without a country
stops.date_confidence: 1632 is attested (mjakub.cz) for his recording as bishop and secretary of the exiled Unity, but other summaries reserve the senior bishopric for his 1648 election; the exact rank conferred in 1632 is not reconciled across sources and is not adjudicated here. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He is recorded as bishop and secretary of the Unity of the Brethren, keeper of its records and its correspondence, at forty. The church he administers has no territory, no legal existence in the land it came from, and congregations scattered across Poland, Hungary, and Silesia. Its archive is a set of boxes in his house. The office is ordinary work: registers, ordinations, letters to Protestant courts, the accounting of who is left alive and where they have settled.
suggested_refs: The archive of the Unity of the Brethren, kept in his house at Leszno until 1656

stops.name: London, Hartlib's house and the college of light
stops.date_confidence: Arrival 21 September 1641 and about nine months in Hartlib's household attested (mjakub.cz); the research pool's geography lens tags the London material [R], drawing on the Oxford DNB entry for Hartlib and the EMLO Hartlib correspondence catalogue. No journey file for Hartlib exists in the corpus; he is named here as a direct associate, not as an interlock.
stops.campa: He lands in England on the twenty-first of September at the invitation of Samuel Hartlib, the Anglo-German projector who has already printed one of his pansophic manuscripts without asking permission. For about nine months he lodges in Hartlib's household while Hartlib, John Dury, Joachim Hubner, and Theodore Haak lobby Parliament for a college of light, an endowed institution to gather all knowledge into one order and teach it. He drafts Via lucis there. Parliament goes to war with its king instead, and he leaves.
suggested_refs: Via lucis, drafted in London 1641-1642, printed at Amsterdam 1668
The Hartlib Papers, University of Sheffield

stops.name: Endegeest, the meeting with Descartes
stops.date_confidence: July 1642 per mjakub.cz; encyclopedia.com places the Netherlands meeting with Descartes in 1642. Day unknown, defaulted. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from rene_descartes.journey.json's own Endegeest stop, dated 1641-1643 there. The elaborate dueling-dialogue versions of the encounter are later embellishment and are not used.
stops.campa: Traveling north to Sweden on Louis de Geer's money, he turns aside to a moated house outside Leiden where Rene Descartes is living, and the two men spend a day together. Descartes is writing replies to the objectors of the Meditations. Comenius is carrying a plan to order all knowledge out of revelation, sense, and reason together. Method is the word both of them use and they do not mean the same thing by it. Later writers stage the meeting as a duel with speeches. What survives is that it happened, and that neither man changed his mind.
suggested_refs: Kasteel Endegeest at Oegstgeest, Descartes's residence 1641-1643

stops.name: Stockholm, Oxenstierna wants schoolbooks
stops.date_confidence: The Stockholm meetings with Oxenstierna are attested (mjakub.cz) within the 1642 journey north; month unknown, defaulted to follow the July Endegeest stop.
stops.campa: Louis de Geer, the Dutch-born merchant who arms the Swedish crown, has paid his way north. In Stockholm he is examined by Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna, who has run Sweden's war for a decade and who wants one thing from him: Latin textbooks, on schedule, for Swedish schools. Comenius wants to explain pansophy. The chancellor is said to have heard him out at length and then returned to the subject of the textbooks, which are what Sweden is buying. The arrangement is settled on those terms.
suggested_refs: The de Geer patronage contract for the Swedish school-reform textbooks

stops.name: Elblag, six years of slipping deadlines
stops.date_confidence: The Elbing period 1642-1648 is attested (mjakub.cz; encyclopedia.com; en.wikipedia, 'Elblag'); month of settlement unknown, defaulted to autumn to follow the Stockholm stop.
stops.campa: He is installed in Royal Prussia rather than in Sweden, in a Baltic port under Swedish influence, with assistants and de Geer's money, to produce the language course he has promised. He works on it. He also works on pansophy, on the reunion of the churches, on the Brethren's correspondence, on the prophecies. Six years pass in a house he did not choose, in a town he has no connection to, writing schoolbooks for the children of a nation not his own out of an arms fortune. The deliverables come late and come short.
suggested_refs: The Elbing Latin textbooks commissioned by de Geer for the Swedish schools

stops.name: Torun, the Colloquium Charitativum
stops.date_confidence: Participation in the preparations and proceedings attested (mjakub.cz; the Comenius and de Geer study published by Brill, cited in the research pool). Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Wladyslaw IV convenes Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed theologians in this Vistula town to see whether the confessions can be brought back into one church. Comenius helps prepare it and takes part. It fails. The strict on every side regard reconciliation as surrender, and Oxenstierna, whose war depends on Protestant Europe staying divided from Catholic Europe, reproaches his contractor for spending Swedish money on peace. He goes on doing it for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Colloquium Charitativum of Thorn, 1645
sources: Brill, study of Comenius and Louis de Geer

segments.name: The Testament of the Dying Mother

stops.name: Leszno, the death of Marie Dorota
stops.date_confidence: August 1648 given by both mjakub.cz and encyclopedia.com; day unknown, defaulted. The third marriage to Jana Gajusova in 1649 is attested by the same source and is folded into this stop rather than given its own.
stops.campa: He is back in Leszno when Marie Dorota Cyrillova dies in August, after twenty-four years and four surviving children: Dorota Kristina, Alzbeta, Zuzana, and Daniel. She had married an outlawed priest in a Bohemian town in 1624 and followed him over a frontier, into Poland, and through the Prussian years. He is fifty-six and has buried two wives and two sons. She is buried in the Brethren ground at Leszno, eight years before the town burns. He marries Jana Gajusova the following year, and she outlives him.
suggested_refs: The Brethren burial ground at Leszno

stops.name: Leszno, Westphalia and the Kshaft
stops.date_confidence: 1648 attested for the Kshaft and for his becoming senior bishop in the common formulation (mjakub.cz); month unknown, set to November to follow the signing of the Peace of Westphalia on 24 October 1648.
stops.campa: The Peace of Westphalia is signed in October and fixes the religion of Europe on the map of 1624. Bohemia and Moravia stay Habsburg and stay Catholic. The Unity of the Brethren is not restored, not tolerated, and not mentioned. Thirty years of war and every prophecy he collected end in a document that leaves the exiles exactly where they are. He answers it with Ksaft umirajici matky, Jednoty bratrske, in which a dying mother wills her goods away: her order to the Lutherans, her discipline to the Reformed, her Bible and her hope to the Czech and Moravian people. He is her bishop and he is writing her will.
suggested_refs: Ksaft umirajici matky, Jednoty bratrske (1650)

stops.name: Sarospatak, the seven-grade school
stops.date_confidence: The invitation from Zsuzsanna Lorantffy and Sigismund Rakoczi and the 1650-1654 Sarospatak period are attested (mjakub.cz; en.wikipedia, 'Sarospatak'); month unknown, defaulted. The Great Didactic line quoted below is Keatinge's rendering of the work's stated main object, placed here for its subject.
stops.campa: Zsuzsanna Lorantffy, widow of the prince of Transylvania, and her son Sigismund Rakoczi bring him to the Reformed college on the Bodrog to rebuild it. He designs a seven-grade pansophic school in which each year is a complete world in itself, wider and deeper than the year before. Three grades are opened. The rest never is. There are not enough masters, not enough books, not enough money, and not enough patience among people who wanted a better Latin school and were handed a system. He stays four years.
stops.quote: To seek and to find a method of instruction, by which teachers may teach less, but learners may learn more.
stops.quote_source: The Great Didactic, statement of the work's main object, tr. M. W. Keatinge (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The Reformed College of Sarospatak and its Comenius rooms

stops.name: Sarospatak, the school played as theatre
stops.date_confidence: Tagged [R] in the research pool: mjakub.cz places the writing or revision of Schola ludus, Praecepta morum, Leges scholae bene ordinatae, and the draft of Orbis sensualium pictus at Sarospatak, without fixing the year of each. 1651 orders the segment; month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He writes Schola ludus here, the school as play: the whole of the Janua turned into Latin dramas that the boys perform, so that the grammar arrives through a body moving on a stage. He drafts Praecepta morum and Leges scholae bene ordinatae, and the book that will outlast all the rest, Orbis sensualium pictus, in which every thing named is also drawn. He is fifty-nine. The pictures are not ornament; they carry the lesson, and the text is keyed to them by number.
stops.quote: Now there is nothing in the understanding, which was not before in the sense. And therefore to exercise the senses well about the right perceiving the differences of things, will be to lay the grounds for all wisdom.
stops.quote_source: Orbis Sensualium Pictus, 'The Author's Preface to the Reader,' English edition, archive.org text
suggested_refs: Schola ludus (1656) and the Sarospatak school dramas

stops.name: Trnava, among the Brethren of the Slovak country
stops.date_confidence: Dated 1651 only to order the segment; mjakub.cz lists Skalica, Trnava, Puchov, Levoca, and Presov among his stops in the 1650-1654 period without a reconstructable itinerary, tagging Skalica [R] and the others [A] in the research pool. Coordinates are Trnava; the other towns are named in the campa but not staged as stops.
stops.campa: From Sarospatak he travels west through the Brethren communities of upper Hungary, the Slovak country: Skalica, Trnava, Puchov, Levoca, Presov, congregations of Czech and Moravian exiles who crossed the same frontier he did and stopped short of Poland. He preaches, inspects schools, ordains. No complete itinerary of these journeys survives, only the list of places. It is the nearest he will come for the rest of his life to the language and the country he was expelled from.
suggested_refs: The Brethren exile congregations of upper Hungary, 1650-1654

stops.name: Lednica, Drabik's revelations
stops.date_confidence: The meeting with Mikulas Drabik in exile is given by mjakub.cz alone; sk.wikipedia's Lednica article mentions neither Drabik nor Comenius, so the [A] tag the research pool carried is too strong and this is recorded as [R]. Coordinates corrected to 49.1047, 18.2167; the pool's 49.0333, 18.3167 lay about 11 km southeast. Year within 1650-1654 and month both unfixed, defaulted to order the segment.
stops.campa: In the Vah valley he finds Mikulas Drabik, whom he knew as a boy at the Straznice school, now an exiled Brethren minister who prophesies. He is sixty, and Drabik is the third visionary he has taken down after Kotter and Poniatowska. He will record Drabik's revelations for twenty years and print them, and the collecting will cost him more among the learned than any book of his repairs. They are wrong in every particular. Drabik's say that the Habsburgs fall, and that the Turks and the Transylvanians bring the Czechs home.
suggested_refs: The Drabik revelations as printed in Lux in tenebris (1657) and Lux e tenebris (1665)

stops.name: Sarospatak, the leaving
stops.date_confidence: Departure in 1654 after conflict with rector Janos Tolnai Dali and other local colleagues over authority and curriculum is attested (mjakub.cz); month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He goes, after four years, over authority and curriculum. The rector, Janos Tolnai Dali, and other local men will not be reorganized by a foreigner with a system, and the seven grades stay at three. The books written here are among the best of his life and the school is a partial failure, and both of those are true at once. He rides back to Leszno, to the town that took in his church twenty-six years earlier, and finds it standing. He is sixty-two.
suggested_refs: The Sarospatak curriculum documents and the surviving records of the dispute with Tolnai Dali

stops.name: Leszno, Cromwell and Charles Gustav
stops.date_confidence: Both events are tagged [R] in the research pool, from mjakub.cz: the 1654 petition to Cromwell by Comenius and Czech exiles, and the 1655 Panegyricus Carolo Gustavo. They are combined into one stop dated 1655; month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He petitions Oliver Cromwell for money and troops toward an alignment of England, Sweden, and Transylvania against the House of Austria. Nothing comes of it. When Charles X Gustav of Sweden invades Poland, he greets the invasion in print with a Panegyricus, putting the Brethren of Leszno publicly on the Swedish side. Drabik's prophecies say this is the turn at last. He signs his name to a Swedish king's arrival in a Polish town, in print, and the town is where his family lives.
suggested_refs: Panegyricus Carolo Gustavo (1655)

stops.name: Leszno, the town burned
stops.date_confidence: 28-29 April 1656 attested (mjakub.cz; the Czech Military History Institute, vhu.cz, cited in the research pool). That Comenius personally caused the burning is not established: responsibility lay with armed forces amid the wider Swedish Deluge.
stops.campa: Swedish fortunes reverse, and Polish forces and local insurgents come to Leszno for what the town did. They burn it. He escapes with his family and loses the rest: his house, his library, the archive of the Unity of the Brethren going back two centuries, the printing resources, and the manuscript of the Czech-Latin Thesaurus, the dictionary of his own language he had worked at for decades. He is sixty-four. It is the second library, and this time the fire is answering something he had done.
suggested_refs: The lost Czech-Latin Thesaurus linguae Bohemicae, burned at Leszno

stops.name: Amsterdam, the city council's stipend
stops.date_confidence: 1656 arrival at Laurens de Geer's invitation and the grant of a regular income and publication subsidies by the city council are attested (mjakub.cz); month unknown, defaulted to follow the April burning and the flight through Silesian and German territory. Coordinates inherited from the canonical Amsterdam pin already used across the corpus.
stops.campa: Laurens de Geer, son of the man who paid for Elbing, brings him to Amsterdam, and the city council grants him a regular income and money to print. After twenty-eight years of patrons, deadlines, and lodgings in other men's houses, a municipal government simply pays him to write. He is sixty-four and has no country, no church with a territory, no library, and, for the first time since Fulnek, no landlord who wants something specific by a date. Amsterdam does not ask him for schoolbooks.
suggested_refs: The Amsterdam city council's grant of income and printing subsidy, 1656

stops.name: Amsterdam, Opera didactica omnia
stops.date_confidence: 1657 Amsterdam publication of the four-part collected didactic works, gathering writing composed between 1627 and 1657, attested (mjakub.cz; the digitized original at mateo.uni-mannheim.de; en.wikipedia, 'Didactica Magna'). Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He gathers thirty years of didactic writing, everything from the Czech Didaktika begun in 1627 to the Sarospatak texts, into four folio parts and dedicates them to the city council that paid for the printing. He is sixty-five. Didactica magna is printed here for the first time, thirty years after he began it. So is the record of every school he tried to build and did not finish: the Leszno gymnasium, the Elbing commission, the seven grades at Sarospatak, the college of light in London.
stops.quote: If a man is to be produced, it is necessary that he be formed by education.
stops.quote_source: The Great Didactic, chapter VI heading, tr. M. W. Keatinge (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: Opera didactica omnia, 4 parts (Amsterdam, 1657), digitized at mateo.uni-mannheim.de

stops.name: Nuremberg, Orbis sensualium pictus
stops.date_confidence: 1658 Nuremberg first edition, Latin and German in parallel, attested (Newberry Library, Digital Collections for the Classroom; en.wikipedia, 'Orbis Pictus'). Month unknown, defaulted. The research pool called the illustrations woodcuts; en.wikipedia describes them as copperplate across 150 chapters, so the medium is left unstated in the campa. The claim that this is the first children's picture book is not made: it is among the earliest systematic illustrated textbooks designed for children.
stops.campa: The picture book appears in Nuremberg, Latin and German in parallel columns, a hundred and fifty chapters, each a numbered scene with the numbers repeated in the text so the eye moves between the drawing and the word. God, air, fish, the tailor, the printing house, the last judgment. Charles Hoole's English follows in 1659, a four-language edition in 1666, a Czech-Latin-German-Hungarian one at Levoca in 1685. It stays in print for a hundred and fifty years, as far as the twelfth London edition of 1810, which doubles as the first American one.
stops.quote: The ground of this business, is, that sensual objects may be rightly presented to the senses, for fear they may not be received.
stops.quote_source: Orbis Sensualium Pictus, 'The Author's Preface to the Reader,' English edition, archive.org text
suggested_refs: Orbis sensualium pictus (Nuremberg, 1658); Charles Hoole's English edition (London, 1659)
sources: Newberry Library, Digital Collections for the Classroom, dcc.newberry.org
Public Domain Review essay on Orbis Pictus

stops.name: Breda, Angelus pacis
stops.date_confidence: Tagged [R] in the research pool: mjakub.cz places him at Breda during the Anglo-Dutch peace negotiations distributing Angelus pacis, and notes the tract carried no formal diplomatic authority. Month unknown, defaulted to the period of the talks; the treaty was signed in July 1667.
stops.campa: England and the Dutch Republic are negotiating an end to their second war, and he comes to Breda with a tract he has had printed and hands it out. Angelus pacis argues that Christian states settling a naval and commercial quarrel by war are ridiculous, and that what is wanted instead is a standing arrangement among nations for judging between them. He holds no commission and represents no power. He is seventy-five. The treaty is signed in July on the terms the two governments had already agreed.
suggested_refs: Angelus pacis (1667), distributed at the Breda negotiations

stops.name: Amsterdam, the unfinished consultation
stops.date_confidence: Death date and age attested (mjakub.cz; encyclopedia.com); no reliable cause of death appears in the principal sources. The 1966 Prague edition is confirmed by cs.wikipedia ('Obecna porada o naprave veci lidskych'): first complete Latin edition, Academia, Prague, 1966, with the first complete Czech translation in 1992. The often-repeated 1934 rediscovery at Halle and a UNESCO Memory of the World inscription could not be confirmed from any source reachable in this pass and are not asserted.
stops.campa: He dies on the fifteenth of November, seventy-eight years old. De rerum humanarum emendatione consultatio catholica, the seven-part work meant to hold everything, panegersia, panaugia, pansophia, pampaedia, panglottia, panorthosia, pannuthesia, is unfinished, and he leaves it to his son Daniel and to Christian Vladislav Nigrinus to complete and print. They do not manage it. The manuscript passes out of sight for centuries, and the first complete Latin edition is published in Prague in 1966. No source gives a cause of death.
suggested_refs: De rerum humanarum emendatione consultatio catholica, first complete Latin edition, Academia, Prague, 1966
sources: cs.wikipedia, 'Obecna porada o naprave veci lidskych'

stops.name: Naarden, the Walloon chapel
stops.date_confidence: Burial one week after death attested (mjakub.cz; Czech Embassy in The Hague, mzv.gov.cz). Reinterment on 25 July 1929 and the 1933-1937 rebuilding as a Czechoslovak-sponsored mausoleum by Ladislav Machon, with glass by Jaroslav Benda, screen and candelabra by Jaroslav Horejc, and woodcarving by Karel Stipl, from nl.wikipedia, 'Comeniusmuseum'. The Naarden museum's founding in 1892 is confirmed by the same source.
stops.campa: He is buried a week after his death in the Walloon Reformed chapel of this Dutch garrison town, among a French-speaking refugee congregation, in a country he reached at sixty-four. Within a generation nobody can say which stone is his. The grave is found again and the remains formally reinterred on the twenty-fifth of July 1929; between 1933 and 1937 the Dutch government transfers the chapel to Czechoslovakia and Ladislav Machon rebuilds it as his mausoleum. The Czech state keeps a grave in Holland because the man in it was never allowed to come home.
suggested_refs: The Comenius Mausoleum in the Walloon chapel at Naarden, and the Comeniusmuseum beside it
sources: Czech Embassy in The Hague, mzv.gov.cz
